rows.evidence: Q1: Methods 2.1-2.3 <U+2013> two-year replicated field experiment (RCBD, 4 reps, 8 treatments) at BISA Ladhowal, Punjab, 2014-16. Q2: Abstract and Section 3.3, Figs. 4-5 <U+2013> irrigation water applied through the (sub)surface drip system was 48-53% lower in rice and 42-53% lower in wheat than flood irrigation under CA, measured with a water meter; Sections 3.5 and 3.6, Tables 4-5 <U+2013> 20% less fertilizer N gave similar yields (higher PFPN) and variable costs including labour were lower under drip than conventional flood. Q8: Section 3.3 <U+2013> authors state further studies are needed to compute full water balance components to report real water savings; Section 3.2 <U+2013> results need evaluation for different soil types, climatic conditions and irrigation availability for wider application; Conclusions <U+2013> a single N rate and fixed 7-day fertigation schedule were used.
rows.notes: Water saving quantified only as metered irrigation input at plot scale (70 m2 plots), one silt loam site, two crops; no second method. Mechanisms (reduced evaporation, deep drainage, percolation) are asserted or cited, not measured; tensiometers used only for scheduling. Residue mulch increased water saving but is reported as a factor the effect varied with, not stated as a requirement. Statistics are LSD/letter groupings; no SD, SE, CI or ranges of replicate data for the water-saving result. The review's context sentence (46.7%/44.7% savings in rice-wheat-mungbean and maize-wheat-mungbean) does not match this study's figures, suggesting the context belongs to another cited paper; the study nonetheless supports the drip+CA water-saving claim.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods 2.1-2.3 <U+2013> two-year replicated field experiment at one site in Punjab, India.
rows.notes: The study measures irrigation water input, grain yield, irrigation water productivity, partial factor productivity of N and net returns under SSDF versus flood irrigation. It does not test resilience or risk management (no drought/stress scenarios, yield stability, or variability analysis); in fact it notes that well-distributed rain in 2015 nullified the drip effect on rice yield. Statements that drip is an option for a water-scarce future and groundwater depletion are discussion/extrapolation. The measured water saving is at most a precondition for the claimed resilience, so upstream is set true.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a single-site, two-year plot experiment on silt loam in NW India; the direct evidence is on irrigation water saving, WPi, N use efficiency and economics of SSDF with CA in rice-wheat, not on resilience/risk.
